topics.title: Matrices: The Machines That Move Vectors
topics.description: A **matrix** is not just a grid of numbers, it's an instruction for how to rotate, stretch, or squash every vector it touches.

lesson.summary: A **matrix** is not just a grid of numbers, it's an instruction for how to rotate, stretch, or squash every vector it touches.
lesson.content:
## Matrices: The Machines That Move Vectors

> **Core Concept:** A **matrix** is not just a grid of numbers, it's an instruction for how to rotate, stretch, or squash every vector it touches.

### Why It Matters
- A vector on its own just sits there, something has to actually reshape or move it to extract useful structure from it.
- ==A single number cannot describe a consistent, repeatable transformation== applied to many different vectors.
- A neural network layer needs a compact way to turn one vector (like raw pixels) into a new, more useful vector (like 'this looks like an edge'), and doing that one number at a time would not scale.

### Intuitive Analogy
Think of a matrix like a cookie cutter press that also happens to warp the dough
as it presses down. You feed in a shape (a vector), and the press does something
consistent to it every single time: maybe it stretches the shape sideways, maybe
it spins it thirty degrees, maybe it flattens it like a pancake. Different presses
do different things, but the same press always treats every piece of dough the
same way. That consistent, repeatable warping is exactly what a matrix does to
vectors.


### Key Engineering Principles
- When people say a matrix 'acts on' a vector, they mean you multiply the matrix by the vector and get a new vector out. Mechanically, each entry of the output is the **dot product** of one row of the matrix with the input vector, so an n-by-m matrix turns an m-dimensional vector into an n-dimensional one.
- Worked example: the matrix [[2, 0], [0, 3]] acting on the vector [1, 1] gives [2 times 1 + 0 times 1, 0 times 1 + 3 times 1] = [2, 3]. Every vector stretches by 2 along the first axis and by 3 along the second, that's a scaling transformation, encoded entirely in the matrix's numbers.
- The interesting part isn't the arithmetic, it's what that new vector looks like compared to the old one, longer or shorter, rotated, flipped, or squashed flat into fewer dimensions.
- Some matrices spin vectors around like a clock hand (rotations), some stretch them longer in one direction while squishing them in another (scaling), some flip them across an axis (reflections), and some barely nudge them at all (close to the identity matrix).
- The matrix itself never changes. It treats every vector you hand it with the exact same rule, rotate this much, stretch that much, which is what makes a matrix a reusable transformation rather than a one-off calculation.
- The **identity matrix**, with 1s down the diagonal and 0s everywhere else, is the 'do nothing' transformation, every vector comes out exactly as it went in. It's the natural reference point for understanding what any other matrix is actually changing.
- That consistency is exactly why matrices are so useful in AI, a neural network layer is basically a matrix (plus a nonlinear twist) that transforms an input vector into a new, hopefully more useful vector, and that same matrix is reused for every input the network ever sees.
- Applying two matrices back to back, first A then B, is itself equivalent to a single combined matrix, computed by multiplying B and A together. This is why deep networks can be thought of as one long chain of transformations, each layer contributing its own matrix to the chain.
- You don't need to calculate matrix multiplication by hand to build the intuition, just remember the shape of the idea: matrix in, vector in, new vector out, and the matrix's numbers are the recipe for exactly how that vector gets reshaped.
- Stack enough of these transformations together, each reshaping the data a little more usefully, and you start to get something that looks like deep learning, raw pixels slowly reshaped, layer by layer, into a representation where 'this is a cat' becomes an easy final step.

topics.description: Instead of only learning FROM real experience, an agent can also **learn a model of the world**, then practice inside its own imagination, planning many extra updates for free.

lesson.summary: Instead of only learning FROM real experience, an agent can also **learn a model of the world**, then practice inside its own imagination, planning many extra updates for free.
lesson.content:
## Model-Based RL and Planning: Learning a Model, Then Thinking Ahead

> **Core Concept:** Instead of only learning FROM real experience, an agent can also **learn a model of the world**, then practice inside its own imagination, planning many extra updates for free.

### Why It Matters
- Model-free methods (Q-learning, DQN, policy gradients) are ==sample-inefficient==, they need enormous amounts of real environment interaction to learn well, which is slow or expensive in the real world.
- Real experience is often costly (a robot's motors wear out, a real trade loses real money), but computation inside a learned model is comparatively cheap.
- You want a way to squeeze more learning out of every real experience, without waiting for more of it.

### Intuitive Analogy
Imagine learning to cook a new dish. The model-free way: cook it for real,
a hundred times, adjusting a little each time based on how it actually
tastes. The model-based way: after just a handful of real attempts, build
up a mental model of how ingredients and techniques combine, then mentally
rehearse dozens of variations in your head before ever touching the stove
again, only cooking for real once your mental simulations point somewhere
promising. You still need real attempts to build the mental model in the
first place, but once you have one, most of the "practice" can happen in
your imagination, for free.


### Key Engineering Principles
- **Model-based RL** learns an explicit model of the environment, M(s, a) predicting the next state and reward, from real experience, then uses that learned model to simulate additional, imagined experience or to plan ahead directly.
- This is a genuinely different idea from Dynamic Programming's model: DP assumed you were GIVEN a perfect model upfront. Here, the agent LEARNS an imperfect, approximate model from its own experience, then plans with it anyway.
- **Dyna** (Sutton's classic architecture) elegantly combines both worlds: after every real step, do a normal model-free update (like Q-learning) AND update the learned model, AND run several extra 'imagined' updates by sampling from the model, squeezing far more learning out of each real interaction.
- The core tradeoff: a learned model is never perfectly accurate, so planning with it risks compounding model errors, especially many steps into an imagined rollout, versus the real efficiency gain of not needing costly real interaction for every single update.
- **Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)** is a different, extremely powerful planning technique: build a search tree of possible future action sequences from the current state, using simulated rollouts to estimate which branches look promising, and focus most of the search effort on the most promising branches (guided by something like UCB, met in the bandits lesson).
- MCTS has four repeating steps: **selection** (walk down the tree toward promising branches), **expansion** (add a new node), **simulation** (roll out a fast, rough estimate from there), **backpropagation** (update every node on the path with the result). Repeat thousands of times before actually committing to a real move.
- MCTS is exactly how classic game-playing AI ==decides its next move in real time==: rather than evaluating the whole game tree exhaustively (impossible for games like Go), it spends its 'thinking time' concentrated on the branches that currently look most promising, refining that focus as more simulations complete.
- **Integrating learning and planning** (Silver's own phrase for this topic) means a modern agent can use BOTH a learned value function or policy (from model-free learning) AND a learned or given model for lookahead planning, combining pattern-recognition with explicit search, which is precisely the recipe behind AlphaGo, the next lesson's case study.
- Planning depth is itself a dial: a shallow, fast rollout policy trades accuracy for speed, letting MCTS run many more simulations in the same time budget, a genuine speed-versus-accuracy tradeoff that real systems tune carefully.

topics.title: Model Evaluation and Overfitting: Memorizing the Answers vs. Learning the Pattern
topics.description: A model that aces its training data but flops on new data hasn't learned anything, it's just ==memorized the answer key==. Testing on unseen data is the only honest way to check.

lesson.summary: A model that aces its training data but flops on new data hasn't learned anything, it's just ==memorized the answer key==. Testing on unseen data is the only honest way to check.
lesson.content:
## Model Evaluation and Overfitting: Memorizing the Answers vs. Learning the Pattern

> **Core Concept:** A model that aces its training data but flops on new data hasn't learned anything, it's just ==memorized the answer key==. Testing on unseen data is the only honest way to check.

### Why It Matters
- A model can look perfect on the data it was trained on and still fail completely on new, real-world data.
- Accuracy alone can be misleading, especially when one outcome is much rarer than the other.
- You need an honest way to tell whether a model actually learned the pattern or just memorized examples.

### Intuitive Analogy
Imagine a student who gets hold of the exact exam questions and answers ahead
of time and memorizes them word for word. They'll score perfectly on that
specific test. Give them a slightly different exam covering the same topic
the next day, and they fall apart, because they never actually learned the
subject, they memorized one specific answer key. A model that overfits is
that student. It looks brilliant on the data it already saw and reveals
nothing until you test it on questions it has never encountered before.


### Key Engineering Principles
- The only fair way to check a model is to test it on data it never saw during training, evaluating on training data answers a different, less useful question.
- Practitioners split data before training, commonly 80% into a **training set** and 20% held back as a **test set**, and often carve out a third validation set for tuning choices along the way without touching the test set.
- Doing well on the untouched test set is real evidence the model learned the underlying pattern, rather than just memorizing specific examples.
- **Overfitting** is learning the training data too well, down to its noise and quirks, rather than the general rule underneath it, ==a big gap between training accuracy and test accuracy== is the tell.
- **Underfitting** is the opposite failure, the model is too simple to capture the real pattern at all, and performs poorly on both training and test data alike.
- **Cross-validation** gives a more reliable read than one single train/test split: split the data into k folds, train on k-1 of them and test on the remaining one, repeat so every fold gets a turn as the test set, then average the scores.
- A **confusion matrix** lays out actual versus predicted outcomes in a small grid: true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives, and every other classification metric is built from those four counts.
- **Precision** asks, of everything the model flagged as positive, how much was actually positive. **Recall** asks, of everything that was actually positive, how much did the model catch. The two usually trade off against each other.
- The **F1 score** combines precision and recall into one number (their harmonic mean), useful as a single summary when you care about both roughly equally and don't want to track two numbers separately.
- Regularization, early stopping, simplifying the model, and gathering more training data are the standard tools for fighting overfitting, adding model complexity or more useful features are the standard tools for fighting underfitting.

topics.title: The Silent Slippage: Monitoring Model Drift
topics.description: A model does not have to change for it to get worse. The world around it changes instead, and if nobody is watching, that decline can go unnoticed for a long time, a phenomenon called **model drift**.

lesson.summary: A model does not have to change for it to get worse. The world around it changes instead, and if nobody is watching, that decline can go unnoticed for a long time, a phenomenon called **model drift**.
lesson.content:
## The Silent Slippage: Monitoring Model Drift

> **Core Concept:** A model does not have to change for it to get worse. The world around it changes instead, and if nobody is watching, that decline can go unnoticed for a long time, a phenomenon called **model drift**.

### Why It Matters
- The world a model was trained on keeps changing after training day, while the model itself stays frozen.
- Drift produces ==no crash and no error message==, so a model can quietly get worse for a long time before anyone notices.
- Trusting launch-day accuracy forever means you have no idea how the model is actually performing right now.

### Intuitive Analogy
Think about a tailor who makes you a suit that fits perfectly the day you pick
it up. Nobody touched the suit after that. But a few years later, after some
changes in your daily habits, it does not sit quite right anymore. The suit is
identical to the day it was made. You are the one who changed, gradually and
without a single dramatic moment you could point to. If you never tried it on
again, you might not notice until it was uncomfortably obvious.


### Key Engineering Principles
- A model is trained on data that reflects the world at one particular moment, but the world does not hold still afterward, and the model's parameters stay frozen at whatever they were the day training ended.
- Customer behavior shifts, language trends change, a competitor changes the market, and the gap between what the model learned and reality quietly widens, one small shift at a time rather than one dramatic break.
- This gradual mismatch is called **model drift**, and it is dangerous precisely because nothing crashes and no error message appears. The system keeps returning confident, well-formatted answers, just increasingly wrong ones.
- **Data drift** is when production inputs start looking statistically different from the data the model was trained on, for example a fraud model trained mostly on desktop purchases suddenly seeing a flood of mobile transactions with different patterns.
- **Concept drift** is when the relationship between inputs and the right answer itself changes, even if the inputs look similar, for example the same search query 'best laptop' meaning something different in trend after a major new release.
- **Label drift** is a related, narrower case where the distribution of the correct answers themselves shifts, like a spam classifier's training data being ninety percent legitimate email while real traffic is now sixty percent spam.
- The fix is ongoing monitoring, tracking real predictions against real outcomes where those outcomes are available, and separately watching the statistical shape of incoming data even when true outcomes are delayed or never arrive.
- A practical drift detector compares a summary statistic, like the mean or a full distribution, of a rolling window of recent production inputs against the same statistic from training data, and flags when the gap crosses a **threshold**.
- Ground truth often lags badly. A loan default model might not know whether a prediction was right for months, so teams also watch proxy signals, like the shape of incoming applications, that arrive immediately.
- When drift shows up, the usual answer is retraining on newer data so the model catches up with the world again, but ==retraining on the wrong slice of new data, or too infrequently, can leave you perpetually one step behind==.

topics.title: Monte Carlo Methods: Learning Purely From Experience
topics.description: Monte Carlo methods throw away the requirement of knowing the environment's rules entirely, they estimate how good a state is just by **playing full episodes and averaging what actually happened**.

lesson.summary: Monte Carlo methods throw away the requirement of knowing the environment's rules entirely, they estimate how good a state is just by **playing full episodes and averaging what actually happened**.
lesson.content:
## Monte Carlo Methods: Learning Purely From Experience

> **Core Concept:** Monte Carlo methods throw away the requirement of knowing the environment's rules entirely, they estimate how good a state is just by **playing full episodes and averaging what actually happened**.

### Why It Matters
- Dynamic programming needed a fully known model of the environment, but most real problems ==never hand you exact transition probabilities==, you only get to actually experience the environment.
- You need a way to estimate value functions purely from lived experience, sample episodes, not from a mathematical model of the world.
- Simply averaging raw outcomes sounds naive, it's not obvious this actually converges to the correct answer.

### Intuitive Analogy
Imagine you want to know your average commute time, but you don't have a
map with exact traffic-light timing and traffic-density models. Instead,
you just drive to work 50 times and record how long each trip actually
took, then average those 50 numbers. No model of the city required, just
real, lived experience, repeated many times, averaged together. That
average genuinely converges toward the true expected commute time the
more trips you record. That is exactly what Monte Carlo methods do for
estimating the value of a state.


### Key Engineering Principles
- **Monte Carlo (MC) methods** estimate value functions by playing complete episodes to the end, then averaging the actual returns observed, no model of the environment's transition probabilities is needed at all, only real or simulated experience.
- This is why MC methods only apply to **episodic** tasks, ones that genuinely terminate (a game ending, a maze finishing), since you need the full episode's return before you can use it, there's no way to bootstrap from a partial episode.
- **First-visit MC** estimates V(s) by averaging the return that followed the FIRST time state s was visited in each episode. **Every-visit MC** instead averages the return following EVERY visit to s within an episode, even if s appears multiple times.
- Both variants are proven to converge to the true value function V(s) as the number of sampled episodes grows, purely from the law of large numbers, no bootstrapping, no model, just averaging real outcomes.
- MC methods have **no bias** from an inaccurate model (since they use only real returns), but they do have **high variance**, since a single episode's return depends on a long, noisy chain of random events all the way to the end.
- **Monte Carlo control** extends this to improving a policy, not just evaluating one: estimate Q(s,a) (not just V(s)) from episodes, then improve the policy greedily (or epsilon-greedily, to keep exploring) based on those estimates, alternating estimation and improvement much like DP's policy iteration.
- Because Monte Carlo control needs to try EVERY action in every state enough times to estimate Q(s,a) reliably, it typically uses an epsilon-greedy policy during data collection (called **on-policy** MC control), never purely greedy, or some state-action pairs would simply never get tried.
- Unlike dynamic programming, Monte Carlo methods don't need to sweep over the entire state space, they only ever touch states that actually show up in sampled episodes, which can be a huge practical advantage in enormous state spaces.
- The core limitation Monte Carlo leaves on the table: you must wait for an ENTIRE episode to finish before learning anything from it, which is slow, sample-inefficient, and impossible for tasks that never naturally end, the exact gap Temporal-Difference learning, the next lesson, closes by learning from incomplete episodes.

pages.title: Monte Carlo Methods: Learning Purely From Experience
pages.content:
## Monte Carlo Methods: Learning Purely From Experience

> **Core Concept:** Monte Carlo methods throw away the requirement of knowing the environment's rules entirely, they estimate how good a state is just by **playing full episodes and averaging what actually happened**.

### Why It Matters
- Dynamic programming needed a fully known model of the environment, but most real problems ==never hand you exact transition probabilities==, you only get to actually experience the environment.
- You need a way to estimate value functions purely from lived experience, sample episodes, not from a mathematical model of the world.
- Simply averaging raw outcomes sounds naive, it's not obvious this actually converges to the correct answer.

### Intuitive Analogy
Imagine you want to know your average commute time, but you don't have a
map with exact traffic-light timing and traffic-density models. Instead,
you just drive to work 50 times and record how long each trip actually
took, then average those 50 numbers. No model of the city required, just
real, lived experience, repeated many times, averaged together. That
average genuinely converges toward the true expected commute time the
more trips you record. That is exactly what Monte Carlo methods do for
estimating the value of a state.


### Key Engineering Principles
- **Monte Carlo (MC) methods** estimate value functions by playing complete episodes to the end, then averaging the actual returns observed, no model of the environment's transition probabilities is needed at all, only real or simulated experience.
- This is why MC methods only apply to **episodic** tasks, ones that genuinely terminate (a game ending, a maze finishing), since you need the full episode's return before you can use it, there's no way to bootstrap from a partial episode.
- **First-visit MC** estimates V(s) by averaging the return that followed the FIRST time state s was visited in each episode. **Every-visit MC** instead averages the return following EVERY visit to s within an episode, even if s appears multiple times.
- Both variants are proven to converge to the true value function V(s) as the number of sampled episodes grows, purely from the law of large numbers, no bootstrapping, no model, just averaging real outcomes.
- MC methods have **no bias** from an inaccurate model (since they use only real returns), but they do have **high variance**, since a single episode's return depends on a long, noisy chain of random events all the way to the end.
- **Monte Carlo control** extends this to improving a policy, not just evaluating one: estimate Q(s,a) (not just V(s)) from episodes, then improve the policy greedily (or epsilon-greedily, to keep exploring) based on those estimates, alternating estimation and improvement much like DP's policy iteration.
- Because Monte Carlo control needs to try EVERY action in every state enough times to estimate Q(s,a) reliably, it typically uses an epsilon-greedy policy during data collection (called **on-policy** MC control), never purely greedy, or some state-action pairs would simply never get tried.
- Unlike dynamic programming, Monte Carlo methods don't need to sweep over the entire state space, they only ever touch states that actually show up in sampled episodes, which can be a huge practical advantage in enormous state spaces.
- The core limitation Monte Carlo leaves on the table: you must wait for an ENTIRE episode to finish before learning anything from it, which is slow, sample-inefficient, and impossible for tasks that never naturally end, the exact gap Temporal-Difference learning, the next lesson, closes by learning from incomplete episodes.

topics.title: Why Use a Team of Agents Instead of Just One
topics.description: One generalist agent trying to do everything is like one employee running an entire company. Sometimes a small team of **specialist agents**, each good at one thing, works better.

lesson.summary: One generalist agent trying to do everything is like one employee running an entire company. Sometimes a small team of **specialist agents**, each good at one thing, works better.
lesson.content:
## Why Use a Team of Agents Instead of Just One

> **Core Concept:** One generalist agent trying to do everything is like one employee running an entire company. Sometimes a small team of **specialist agents**, each good at one thing, works better.

### Why It Matters
- A single agent handling an entire complicated task has to be good at everything that task requires: researching, writing, and checking its own work, all at once.
- As a task grows, one agent juggling every responsibility tends to ==lose focus==, and errors in one part of the job bleed into every other part.
- Without splitting work by specialty, an agent's prompt and tools have to cover too much ground to be excellent at any single piece.

### Intuitive Analogy
Imagine a small company where one person is expected to be the accountant,
the salesperson, the customer support rep, and the delivery driver, all at
once. They'd technically get everything done eventually, but they'd be
constantly switching hats, none of the work would get their full focus, and
mistakes would creep in wherever they're weakest. A real company instead
hires an accountant who's actually good with numbers, a salesperson who's
actually good with people, and a driver who knows the routes, then has them
coordinate through a manager who assigns work and keeps everyone pointed at
the same goal. Multi-agent systems copy that second setup.


### Key Engineering Principles
- A single agent handling a large task must be good at everything that task requires inside one continuous train of thought, one prompt trying to cover research, writing, and checking all at once.
- That's doable for smaller tasks, but as a task grows, one agent juggling every responsibility tends to lose focus the same way a person would, since its context fills up with details from every different kind of subtask.
- A multi-agent system splits the work across several agents, each with a narrower job and often a more specialized prompt or set of tools, so each agent's context stays focused on exactly what it needs.
- One agent might specialize in searching for information, another in writing, another in reviewing output for mistakes before it goes out. Each can be tuned, prompted, and even given different tools for its one job.
- **Coordination** is what makes this work instead of turning into chaos, usually through a manager or **orchestrator** agent that assigns pieces and combines results into a single coherent output.
- Without that coordination, a group of independent agents is just several people randomly doing unrelated things in the same room, producing pieces that were never meant to fit together.
- Agents can be arranged in different **topologies**: a hierarchy with one orchestrator directing several workers, or a more peer-to-peer setup where agents pass work directly to each other without a central manager.
- This tradeoff isn't free: more agents means ==more communication overhead==, more places for a mistake to hide, and more cost in tokens and time, so a single well-built generalist agent is often simpler and better for smaller tasks.
- Specialist agents also make debugging easier in one specific way: when something goes wrong, you can usually tell which agent produced the bad output, instead of untangling one long, tangled reasoning trace.
- **Handoffs** between agents are a real design decision. What exactly does the researcher pass to the writer, raw notes or a structured summary, and that choice affects how well the next agent can actually use it.

topics.title: Multi-Armed Bandits: The Simplest RL Problem
topics.description: Before an agent ever has to worry about states changing, it has to solve a purer problem first: **which option do I try, when I don't yet know which one is best, and every trial costs something?**

lesson.summary: Before an agent ever has to worry about states changing, it has to solve a purer problem first: **which option do I try, when I don't yet know which one is best, and every trial costs something?**
lesson.content:
## Multi-Armed Bandits: The Simplest RL Problem

> **Core Concept:** Before an agent ever has to worry about states changing, it has to solve a purer problem first: **which option do I try, when I don't yet know which one is best, and every trial costs something?**

### Why It Matters
- Full reinforcement learning has states, transitions, and delayed rewards all tangled together, which makes it hard to isolate the ==exploration vs exploitation== tension in its purest form.
- An agent that always picks its current favorite option can get permanently stuck on a mediocre choice it happened to try first.
- An agent that keeps trying everything forever wastes reward on options it already has good reason to believe are worse.

### Intuitive Analogy
Imagine walking into a casino with 5 slot machines (the "arms" of a
multi-armed bandit), each with a different, unknown payout rate. You have
100 coins to spend. Pull the same machine every time and you might be
stuck on a bad one forever. Try every machine equally and you waste coins
on the bad ones long after you had good reason to suspect they were bad.
The real skill is spending your early coins learning which machines look
promising, then spending your later coins mostly on the best one you've
found, while never fully ruling out a pleasant surprise.


### Key Engineering Principles
- A **multi-armed bandit** is the simplest possible reinforcement learning problem: there is no state at all, just a fixed set of actions (arms), each with its own unknown, fixed reward distribution. Pull an arm, get a reward, repeat.
- This is Sutton & Barto's own starting point for the entire book, precisely because it isolates the **exploration-exploitation dilemma** without any of the complexity of states or delayed consequences getting in the way.
- **Q(a)**, the action-value here, is just the true expected reward of pulling arm a. The agent doesn't know these values, it only has estimates built from what it's observed so far, written **Q_t(a)**.
- **Greedy** action selection always picks the arm with the highest current estimate. It's pure exploitation, and it can permanently lock onto a suboptimal arm if early luck made a worse arm look good at first.
- **Epsilon-greedy** (already met in earlier lessons) fixes this crudely: mostly exploit, but explore randomly some fraction epsilon of the time. It works, but it explores blindly, a clearly-bad arm gets exactly the same exploration chance as a clearly-promising one.
- **Optimistic initialization** is a cheap, clever trick: start every arm's estimate artificially high. Since every real reward will disappoint that inflated estimate, the agent naturally tries every arm early on, pure exploration, no randomness needed, that fades out on its own.
- **Upper Confidence Bound (UCB)** explores smarter: pick the arm maximizing Q_t(a) + c * sqrt(ln(t) / N_t(a)), where N_t(a) is how many times arm a has been tried. An arm tried rarely gets a big uncertainty bonus, one tried often gets almost none, so exploration automatically concentrates on arms that are both promising AND under-tested.
- **Thompson sampling** takes a Bayesian view: keep a full probability distribution over each arm's likely true value (not just a point estimate), sample one guess from each arm's distribution, and pull whichever arm's sample is highest. Arms you're uncertain about naturally get sampled a wide range of possible values, which itself drives exploration.
- **Regret** is the standard way to score a bandit strategy: the gap between the reward you'd have gotten always pulling the best arm, and the reward you actually got. A good strategy has regret that grows slower and slower over time (ideally logarithmically), a bad strategy (like fixed epsilon-greedy) keeps accumulating regret at a constant rate forever, since it never stops exploring randomly.
- **Contextual bandits** add one piece of MDP machinery back in: a state (context) that varies each round and affects which arm is best, but your action still doesn't change what state comes next. This is the natural stepping stone to full MDPs, the topic of the next lesson, where actions finally do influence the future state too.

topics.title: Multi-Head Attention: More Than One Way to Pay Attention
topics.description: One attention pass can only track one kind of relationship at a time, so transformers run **several in parallel**, each noticing something different.

lesson.summary: One attention pass can only track one kind of relationship at a time, so transformers run **several in parallel**, each noticing something different.
lesson.content:
## Multi-Head Attention: More Than One Way to Pay Attention

> **Core Concept:** One attention pass can only track one kind of relationship at a time, so transformers run **several in parallel**, each noticing something different.

### Why It Matters
- Language has many kinds of relationships happening in the same sentence at once, like grammar structure and pronoun references.
- A single attention pass settles on one lens for viewing relationships, so it cannot capture all of these at once.
- Asking one attention computation to do everything means some relationships get underweighted or missed entirely.

### Intuitive Analogy
Imagine a single detective investigating a case completely alone. They are
decent, but they can only focus on one angle at a time: today they chase the
timeline, tomorrow they check alibis, the day after they examine physical
evidence. A lot gets missed simply because one person cannot hold every
angle in their head simultaneously. Now imagine instead you send in a team
of specialists at the same time: one only tracks the timeline, one only
checks alibis, one only examines evidence, one only interviews witnesses.
They all look at the exact same case file, but each one notices different
things, and afterward they combine their notes into one final report that
is far sharper than any single detective could have produced alone.


### Key Engineering Principles
- A single self-attention pass computes one set of relevance scores between words, which means it settles on essentially one lens for viewing relationships.
- Language has many kinds of relationships in the same sentence: subject to verb, adjective to noun, pronoun to the word it refers back to, and more, all at once.
- **Multi-head attention** runs several self-attention passes side by side at the same time, each with its own separate learned query, key, and value weight matrices.
- Crucially, the heads do not each get a full-size copy of the word's representation. The model's total dimension is ==split evenly across the heads==, so 8 heads on a 512-dimensional model each work with 64 dimensions, keeping the total compute roughly the same as one big head.
- One head might specialize in tracking grammatical structure, another in pronoun references, another in something less easy to name in plain English.
- None of this specialization is hand designed. It emerges on its own during training, the same way each detective naturally drifts toward the angle they are best at, purely because it reduces the training loss to do so.
- After all the heads finish, their outputs are **concatenated** back together into one vector of the original full dimension, then passed through one more learned weight matrix that mixes the heads' information together.
- That final mixing matrix matters: without it, the heads' outputs would just sit side by side unconnected, this step is what lets the model combine insights from different heads into a single coherent representation.
- This is why multi-head attention consistently outperforms a single attention pass of the same total size, splitting the same budget across several independent lenses covers more angles of the same sentence at once.
- Some heads turn out to be far more important than others. Later research found that many heads in a trained model can be pruned away after training with only a small drop in performance, suggesting real redundancy exists alongside the genuine specialization.

topics.title: Classification vs Detection: What's There, and Where
topics.description: Classification answers 'what is in this image.' Detection answers 'what is in this image, and exactly where.'

lesson.summary: Classification answers 'what is in this image.' Detection answers 'what is in this image, and exactly where.'
lesson.content:
## Classification vs Detection: What's There, and Where

> **Core Concept:** Classification answers 'what is in this image.' Detection answers 'what is in this image, and exactly where.'

### Why It Matters
- Knowing an image contains a pedestrian is not enough for a self-driving car. It needs to know exactly where that pedestrian is to decide whether to brake.
- A single photo can contain many objects at once, and a single 'what's in this image' label can't describe each one separately.
- Some applications, like security cameras, genuinely need location, not just presence, and classification alone has no way to provide it.

### Intuitive Analogy
Imagine two different ways someone could describe the contents of your fridge.
The first person says "there's milk, eggs, and leftovers in there somewhere."
Useful, but vague. The second person opens the fridge and points, saying "milk
is on the top shelf, back left. Eggs are in the door rack, second row. Leftovers
are in the container on the middle shelf, right side." The second answer tells
you not just what exists, but exactly where to reach for it. Classification is
the first person. Object detection is the second.


### Key Engineering Principles
- Image classification takes a whole photo and outputs a single label, or a short ranked list of labels with confidence scores, like 'this photo contains a dog.'
- Classification doesn't care how many dogs there are, where in the frame they sit, or what else might also be in the photo. No location information at all, just a global judgment about the whole image.
- Object detection finds every object of interest, draws a tight box around each one called a **bounding box**, and labels what's inside that box, usually described by its top-left corner plus a width and height, or by its two opposite corners.
- A single photo can come back with several separate detection answers, like 'dog, box here,' 'person, box here,' 'bicycle, box over there,' each with its own label and its own confidence score.
- Detection answers 'what' and 'where' at once, for potentially many objects in the same image, not just one label for the whole picture, and the number of detected objects varies photo to photo.
- Under the hood, most detection systems still use the same convolutional building blocks as classification. A shared backbone extracts feature maps first, then separate branches predict box coordinates and class labels from those same features.
- Two-stage detectors first propose a set of candidate regions that might contain an object, then classify and refine each proposed region separately, which tends to be more accurate but slower.
- One-stage detectors skip the separate proposal step and predict boxes and classes directly across the whole image in a single pass, which trades a little accuracy for much faster speed, important for real-time use like video.
- Because a detector can propose multiple overlapping boxes around the same real object, a cleanup step called **non-max suppression** removes the redundant, lower-confidence duplicates and keeps only the best box per object.
- Detection models are typically graded using **intersection over union**, a score that measures how much a predicted box overlaps with the true box, a prediction only counts as correct if that overlap clears some minimum threshold.

topics.title: Stop Flying Blind: Observability for AI Systems
topics.description: Once a model is live and answering real requests, you cannot just watch it work. You need **logs, traces, and metrics** so you can see what it is doing without staring at the code.

lesson.summary: Once a model is live and answering real requests, you cannot just watch it work. You need **logs, traces, and metrics** so you can see what it is doing without staring at the code.
lesson.content:
## Stop Flying Blind: Observability for AI Systems

> **Core Concept:** Once a model is live and answering real requests, you cannot just watch it work. You need **logs, traces, and metrics** so you can see what it is doing without staring at the code.

### Why It Matters
- A model running in production is a black box from the outside, a request goes in and a response comes out with ==nothing visible in between==.
- Without deliberate visibility, the first sign of a real problem is usually an angry user, which is the most expensive way to find out.
- When something is slow or wrong for one specific request, there is no way to know where the time or the failure actually happened.

### Intuitive Analogy
A pilot flying at night over open ocean cannot lean out the window to check
how things are going. They fly by instruments: altitude, speed, fuel
remaining, engine temperature, all displayed on a dashboard that turns an
invisible situation into numbers a human can act on. Nobody would trust a
pilot who said "I will just look outside and get a feel for it." The
instruments exist precisely because a feeling is not good enough when the
cost of being wrong is high.


### Key Engineering Principles
- **Observability** is the deliberate practice of building visibility into a live system, instead of only finding out something broke when a user complains. It is a property you design in, not something you bolt on after an incident.
- **Logs** are a record of individual events as they happen, like 'request received', 'cache miss', or 'model returned an error', each with a timestamp. They answer 'what exactly happened' for a specific moment in time.
- **Metrics** are numbers tracked over time, like average response time or requests per minute, which let you spot trends and set alerts. They are cheap to store precisely because they are aggregated, a metric does not remember any single request.
- **Traces** follow a single request through the entire system, showing exactly which steps it passed through and how long each one took, often visualized as a waterfall of nested spans, one span per step the request touched.
- Metrics tell you something is wrong right now, across the whole system. Traces tell you exactly where, for one specific request. You typically notice a problem through metrics, then use a trace to find its exact cause.
- For AI systems specifically, observability includes AI-native signals beyond typical software metrics: token counts, cost per request, time to first token, and the actual prompt and completion text for debugging bad outputs.
- An **alert** turns a metric crossing some threshold into a notification a human actually sees, ideally before users notice. A metric nobody is alerted on is really just a chart quietly filling up disk space.
- **Percentile latency** matters more than average latency for user experience. The p50 (median) can look perfectly healthy while ==the p99, the slowest one percent of requests, is in serious trouble== and quietly frustrating a real slice of users.
- None of the three, logs, metrics, or traces, replace each other. They answer different questions at different levels of detail, and are strongest used together rather than any one alone.
- A dashboard only helps if someone actually looks at it before things break, not just after a complaint comes in, which is why alerting and on-call rotations matter as much as the dashboard itself.
